name: Hassan Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Hassan, thanks for seeing me. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. This is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Dave Morley, he's got a small firm, just him, his son Lee and me. We do loft conversions and back extensions round the town, old terraced houses mostly. Dave picks me up at seven in the van outside the chip shop on Market Street, and I'm stripping out, carrying timber up ladders, fixing joists, boarding, clearing up. I like the quiet ones where it's just us and the radio, and the customer brings tea.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and how are things with money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Lofts in summer, honestly, it's like an oven up there. And I'm still not great at the fiddly stuff, Dave does the stairs and the roof windows, I'm not trusted with those yet. Money's tight. I live with my girlfriend Nina, she works at the supermarket, we rent a flat above a phone shop. We've got about a fortnight's worth saved, and when Dave has a quiet week, I don't get paid for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. I mean, that's what I'd guess anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, leave us to it. I'd probably say it to Dave in the van and he'd say he's been saying that for years. I don't go online much, maybe the odd comment on the town page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, nothing changes for me. I don't use any of that stuff, never have. Lofts are lofts, every house is different, and I can't see a computer climbing a ladder with a sheet of ply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep working for Dave, keep learning, maybe get to do my first set of stairs this year if he lets me. Try and put a bit by when the work's steady, but that's what I always say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would getting trusted with the stairs mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot, honestly. Dave did his first stairs at nineteen, I'm twenty-seven and still on the boarding. It'd mean I'm actually becoming a carpenter, not just the lad who carries stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything worrying you right now, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dave's sixty-one. When he packs in, does Lee keep me on? Lee's all right, but he's not his dad. That's the thing I think about on the drive home, not robots.

S0.say: Good, leave us to it. I'd say it to Dave in the van and he'd say he's been saying that for years, and maybe I'd leave the odd comment on the town page.
S0.think: Nothing changes for me. I don't use any of that stuff, lofts are lofts, and I can't see a computer climbing a ladder with a sheet of ply.
S0.do: Keeps working for Dave, keeps learning and hopes to be trusted with his first set of stairs this year. Tries to save a bit when work is steady, as he always intends.
S0.feel: Calm; it feels the same as now.
S0.quote: I can't see a computer climbing a ladder with a sheet of ply.
S0.fieldNote: Hassan is quiet and practical, with his real worry being his 61-year-old boss retiring, not technology. Being trusted with stairs is his marker of becoming a real carpenter. He never uses AI and shows no curiosity about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. Strong change. Okay. I'm not sure what that'd look like for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not going to hit small firms like ours, it's the big sites and the offices. People still want a bloke they can trust in their loft. That's what I'd tell anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't know. Dave's started getting quotes off some app that does the drawings, he showed me on his phone. If he can price jobs faster, maybe we get more work, or maybe the big firms get even cheaper and we lose out. I can't tell which.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going like normal and see what happens. If Dave wanted me to learn something, I'd do it, but I'm not going looking. Maybe I'd try harder to save, cut down on the takeaways and the betting app, twenty quid a week or so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a noise in the van engine you keep ignoring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn if Dave asked. What if he asked you to use an AI app on your phone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be useless at first, I'm not going to pretend. I've got an old phone and I don't even do online banking, Nina does it. I'd probably get Lee to do it and just carry on with the boarding. That's honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the betting app. How much does that matter to the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than it should, if I'm honest. Not mad money, ten, twenty a week on the football. Nina hates it. In this picture, that'd probably be the first thing to go, because I'd feel like I should be careful.

S1.say: It's not going to hit small firms like ours, it's the big sites and the offices. People still want a bloke they can trust in their loft.
S1.think: I honestly don't know. Dave already uses an app to do drawings for quotes, and I can't tell whether that means more work for us or the big firms getting even cheaper and taking it.
S1.do: Keeps going as normal and waits to see what happens, learning new things only if Dave asks. Tries to save about twenty a week by cutting takeaways and his football betting.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like an engine noise he keeps ignoring.
S1.quote: I'd probably get Lee to do it and just carry on with the boarding. That's honest.
S1.fieldNote: His public line is that small firms are safe; privately he isn't sure and admits he can't read which way it goes. He'd hand any tech task to the boss's son. A small betting habit is the first thing he'd cut, which he volunteers without being pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's... yeah. That's mental. Is that real?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they've lost the plot, and somebody needs to slow it down. I'm not big on politics, but you can't just switch everyone off. I'd say that down the pub, not online, I don't do online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think I'm finished in this trade. I'm the lad who carries stuff, and that's the first thing a robot does. Dave might keep going for a bit on his name, but he'd keep Lee, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent and food, straight away. If Dave let me go, I'd probably ask my uncle about the warehouse, but that'd go too, wouldn't it. Nina and I would end up back at her mum's in the spare room, that's the only plan I've actually got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, panicky. Like I'm stood on a roof and the ladder's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask about the warehouse, but then that it'd go too. What else would you try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. That's the problem. I've only done labouring, the chippy and this. I'm not going to suddenly learn computers in two years. I'd sign on, I suppose, and see what the government does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Nina that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nothing at first. I'd go quiet, she knows when I go quiet. Then she'd ask, and I'd say I think I'm done at Dave's, and she'd say we'll figure it out. She's better at that than me.

S2.say: They've lost the plot and somebody needs to slow it down. You can't just switch everyone off, and I'd say that down the pub, not online.
S2.think: I'd think I'm finished in this trade. I'm the lad who carries stuff, which is the first thing a robot does, and Dave would keep his son, not me.
S2.do: Stops all spending except rent and food immediately. Asks his uncle about warehouse work, but expects to sign on and move into his girlfriend's mum's spare room.
S2.feel: Panicky, like standing on a roof after the ladder has gone.
S2.quote: I'm the lad who carries stuff, and that's the first thing a robot does.
S2.fieldNote: Hassan has no plan beyond moving in with family and signing on, and he knows it. He can't think of a second option and won't pretend he'd learn computers. He tends to go quiet under stress and relies on his partner to steady things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better than two. Still quick, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to sort it, so somebody should. The government, the big companies, whoever's in charge. I don't really know who, but somebody's meant to be steering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd hope I could get good enough in five years that Dave or Lee couldn't do without me. Stairs, roof windows, the lot. But if robots are coming for hands-on work by the end, it's still the same problem, just later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Dave straight out to teach me the stairs and the roof windows this year. I'd try to save properly, maybe fifty a week when work's on, and get the betting app off my phone. I'd keep going with Dave and hope he lasts five more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad, honestly. I'd be lying awake thinking about it, even with the five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning something completely different with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Driving, my cousin drives for a builder's merchant. But that's going to be robots too, isn't it, the lorries. I keep coming back to not knowing what's safe. So I'd rather get good at what I'm already doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should be steering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, the government, I suppose, but they're all the same lot whoever wins. Maybe the companies that make the robots, since they're making the money. I'm not the best person to ask, I just want someone to have a plan.

S3.say: There's time to sort it, so somebody should, whether it's the government or the big companies. I don't really know who, but somebody's meant to be steering.
S3.think: I'd hope to get good enough in five years that Dave or Lee couldn't do without me. But if robots take hands-on work by the end, it's the same problem, just later.
S3.do: Asks Dave to teach him stairs and roof windows this year and tries to save about fifty a week when work is on. Deletes the betting app and stays with Dave, hoping he lasts five more years.
S3.feel: Losing sleep over it, even with five years' notice.
S3.quote: I keep coming back to not knowing what's safe. So I'd rather get good at what I'm already doing.
S3.fieldNote: Even with five years, Hassan wants to dig in and get better at his current work rather than switch. He can't name a safe alternative and doesn't know who should act, just that someone should. He loses sleep, which marks a real step up from the slower changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Okay. That's a long time in this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time, so there's no excuse for people getting dumped. I'd probably say it once in the pub and then get on with my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I'd probably be a proper carpenter by then, maybe running jobs for Lee. And the end still comes, but that's a long way off. I've never planned ten years ahead in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with Dave, learn the stairs and the roof windows, and try and get a trade certificate at college one day a week if Dave would let me. I'd save what I can, maybe start with twenty a week and build it up. Anything bigger, I'd wait and see what other people are doing first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit worried, at the back of my mind. But I'd still be getting up for work, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never planned ten years ahead. Would this make you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit. Nina would make me. She's got a spreadsheet for our bills, I've never opened it. With ten years' warning she'd have me sat down with it, I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any point in the ten years where you'd change course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Dave retires and Lee lets me go, that'd be the moment. Then I don't know, maybe I'd go on a big site and see what they're doing with the robots. But I'd be pushed, I wouldn't jump.

S4.say: Ten years is loads of time, so there's no excuse for people getting dumped. I'd probably say it once in the pub and then get on with my day.
S4.think: Ten years means I'd probably be a proper carpenter by then, maybe running jobs for Lee. The end still comes, but it's a long way off, and I've never planned ten years ahead in my life.
S4.do: Keeps working for Dave, learns stairs and roof windows and asks to attend college one day a week for a trade certificate. Starts saving about twenty a week and waits to see what others do before any bigger moves.
S4.feel: Worried at the back of his mind, but still getting up for work as usual.
S4.quote: She's got a spreadsheet for our bills, I've never opened it.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Hassan settle into getting better at his trade, his comfort zone. He'd only change course if pushed by Dave retiring and Lee letting him go. His partner is the planner in the household, which he admits with some humour.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Because I'd have nothing, I'm not trained up, I've got two weeks of money and I'd be in Nina's mum's spare room. What would help is somebody actually having a plan, the government I suppose, so people like me get paid while we find something, and get told what's actually safe to learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the small firms. Everyone talks about big companies, but there's thousands of blokes like Dave with a van and a lad. If it goes bad, nobody's going to notice us go.

headlineQuote: There's thousands of blokes like Dave with a van and a lad. If it goes bad, nobody's going to notice us go.
portrait: Hassan Diaz is a 27-year-old carpenter's mate in a three-man firm doing loft conversions, living with his supermarket-worker girlfriend over a phone shop with about two weeks of savings. He never uses AI, relies on his partner for anything online, and measures progress by whether his boss trusts him with stairs. A stall changes nothing for him and steady change leaves him uneasy but waiting. AGI by 2028 leaves him panicked with no plan beyond signing on and moving into a spare room, while five and ten years push him to dig in and get better at the trade he already has. He wants someone in charge to have a plan.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have no training, two weeks of money and would end up in his girlfriend's mum's spare room.
whatWouldHelp: Someone, probably the government, having a plan that pays people while they look for work and tells them what's actually safe to learn.
